item.title: The Incomplete Stories That Hold Families Together
item.description:
Denial

The Incomplete Stories That Hold Families Together

Ann Patchett’s 'Whistler' explores the gentle evolution of shared memory.

Posted June 28, 2026

Key points
  • Anna Freud suggested that denial can sometimes be a necessary part of healthy development.
  • Family stories often serve as adaptive shelters, not outright lies, until deeper truths can be faced.
  • Therapy often brings people back to stories they have told about themselves for decades.

Sigmund Freud described denial as one of the ego's defenses against intolerable psychological pain. His daughter, Anna Freud, expanded this idea, suggesting that denial can sometimes be a necessary and adaptive part of healthy development rather than simply a pathological symptom. We often think of denial as something to overcome, but from a psychological perspective, it can also serve as a temporary shelter until we are emotionally prepared to face a more difficult reality.

While psychoanalytic theorists have traditionally understood denial as an intrapsychic defense, relational and family therapists like me are often equally interested in the stories families create together. Families don't simply pass down memories; they pass down narratives. These shared stories help regulate anxiety and shape how family members understand themselves, one another, and the events that define them. They are rarely outright lies. More often, they are incomplete.

Exploring Family Narratives in Ann Patchett's 'Whistler'

Ann Patchett's enchanting new novel Whistler can be read through this lens. At its heart, the novel explores one family's shared narrative and what happens when its members become emotionally ready to revisit the unfinished parts of the stories they have carried since childhood.

Our protagonist, Daphne, is immediately lovable and relatable. The novel begins when she unexpectedly encounters an important figure from her past, setting into motion a gradual reexamination of her childhood alongside her sister, her husband, and several other key figures. Rather than uncovering shocking secrets, Daphne slowly revises her understanding of experiences she has carried with her for decades. The story unfolds less like a mystery than an emotional excavation, with each conversation peeling back another layer of meaning.

The Psychological Purpose of Incomplete Family Stories

What makes Whistler so psychologically compelling is that Patchett never suggests Daphne's childhood understanding was false. As children, we construct narratives that help us make sense of experiences we are not yet developmentally equipped to fully understand. Families often do the same. The stories they tell—and sometimes the stories they avoid telling—serve an important purpose. They help contain anxiety until everyone is capable of tolerating greater complexity.

As Daphne revisits a dramatic accident from her past, she isn't simply discovering facts that were hidden from her. She is developing the capacity to hold a fuller, richer, and more nuanced version of the truth. Equally important, the other members of her family are becoming ready to do the same. Together, they co-create a new understanding of themselves and of one another.

One of Patchett's greatest strengths is that she allows this transformation to unfold without judgment. There are no villains, no saints, and no tidy psychological explanations. Instead, she portrays deeply decent people doing the best they could with the emotional resources they had at the time. As readers, we are invited to extend the same compassion to them that therapists hope to extend to the individuals, couples, and families we have the honor to work with.

Revisiting Old Narratives for Healing

Therapy often brings people back to stories they have told about themselves for decades. We sometimes imagine that healing comes from uncovering long-hidden secrets. More often, it comes from developing the emotional capacity to revisit familiar stories with new eyes. The facts may not change, but our ability to hold them does.

Perhaps that is Whistler's greatest psychological insight. Sometimes healing isn't learning that our childhood story was wrong. It's becoming emotionally ready to discover that it was incomplete.

item.title: Zen and the Art of Psychedelic Psychotherapy
item.description:
Therapy

Zen and the Art of Psychedelic Psychotherapy

How patience and compassion build resilience and can lead to a life of thriving.

Posted June 28, 2026

Key points
  • Psychedelic psychotherapy often builds our capacity to sit with difficult experiences as a means for growth.
  • There are considerable overlapping practices in both Zen and psychedelic psychotherapy.
  • Bearing witness to our own pain builds our capacity for self-compassion.

In its essence, Zen practice is “waiting purposelessly in a state of the highest tension” as Eugene Herrigel’s teacher taught as captured in Zen in the Art of Archery.

What a sentiment! As it is so difficult to be patient during our greatest times of stress. Most of us can barely tolerate a little anxiety or sadness, or even just being quiet, let alone staying in those feelings “without purpose.” But in truth, it is this very tolerance that builds the resilience we hope to have as we traverse life. Our thriving actually depends on being able to not only tolerate distress but transform because of it.

People come to me hoping psychedelic psychotherapy is the magic bullet for their pain, and they rarely hear me when I say it’s the start of their healing journey and it will more likely bring up all their deepest pain to the surface before growth happens. They would rather believe the hype that psychedelics are a cure-all. They are not. They expose what is hidden, so that we may learn to tend to ourselves the way we were not tended to when the pain happened. Psychedelics often help shift our perspective and allow for some detachment to our old narratives and beliefs that keep us stuck in destructive and harmful loops. They may induce feelings of belonging, bliss, love, awe, wonder, and even the underlying truth of our non-separateness from all existence: that we are everything, everywhere, at once. But human conditioning, and even our attachment to our own suffering tends to last much longer than the session.

The Healing Process: Patience Over Quick Fixes

When I try to explain this before we even begin our preparation work, I am often met with eyes glazed, staring into a future of unlimited treasures and no pain! It is hard to convince a mind yearning for freedom of pain that being with our pain is the answer. And yes, our suffering can indeed soften, loosen, lessen, reduce, and become quieter and less frequent. This is true for those who do their work after the sessions end. But it is the work, and our dedication to our freedom and peace that does this, not the substance itself.

This is where patience comes in. This is where Zen and psychedelics meet, in the purposeless waiting. We are not holding tightly through our anxiety for the anxiety to end. We live our life, being moved forward by our personal mission and values, whatever those may be, while anxiety, sadness, grief, or anger, just to name a few states, are present. We stop reaching for whatever we used previously to temporarily avoid difficult feelings, be it alcohol, drugs, sex, shopping, food, etc. Through the psychedelic psychotherapy process, we begin to learn to tolerate the flood of what’s present. So hard to do! And such a worthwhile endeavor, and this is precisely where we become strong in our cravings, or while being flooded by intense emotions, thoughts, and sensations that have often trapped us. This gift of waiting, or patience, just as when we sit on a meditation cushion and outlast what wants to steal our attention, is the new foundation for moving our life in the direction of our dreams, and toward thriving.

Building Resilience and Compassion Through Psychedelic Psychotherapy

People don’t come to me to stay in survival mode. When done well, psychedelic psychotherapy helps build tenacity and resilience because the pain is brought to the forefront and we learn to have compassion for what surfaces and patience as it moves through us. During a session, we are both witness to whatever arises in the mind, body, and in the room, and the one experiencing it all. We can work with the material therapeutically, as well as simply be a loving witness whose boundaries are sometimes as big as the universe itself. We begin to build our capacity to be with our own pain, while simultaneously applying the salve of love that we often crave from others, but rarely give ourselves. Compassion also arises naturally for our own suffering because we are no longer caught in the stream of a wounded and constricted consciousness (our default network operates subconsciously demanding we always place our attention on what it finds most important, and for those of us in deep psychological and spiritual pain that is often our traumas and wounds.)

Zen and psychedelic psychotherapy are not just practices, but ways of being, where loving awareness and compassion become baseline traits of our consciousness. So that when our suffering arises, we bear witness and tend to old thought patterns, distressing emotions, and constricting sensations with tenderness and love. Our awareness itself naturally contains those medicines.

And all the while we may find there is deep stillness and a quietude under all of these experiences of being human. The more we soften and loosen our hold, surrender and release control, the more likely it is we may touch the deepest peace we have been seeking all along. And it can happen while life is being lived, no matter the circumstances we face.

item.title: Romantic Love Has Become Our New Religion
item.description:
Relationships

Romantic Love Has Become Our New Religion

We hope to be made whole by another rather than by the divine.

Posted June 28, 2026

Key points
  • Love has not always meant what it means today.
  • Romantic love gradually took on the role once played by religion.
  • Understanding love's history illuminates the true meaning of love.
The Sacrifice of Isaac, by Caravaggio
Source: Wikimedia Commons/Michelangelo Merisi da Caravaggio/Public Domain.

Many of us expect love to do far more than make us happy. We expect it to make us whole, to tell us who we are, and even to give our lives meaning. This understanding of love is surprisingly recent.

Love is a word with a meaning that has changed over the centuries. Today, we tend to think about love primarily in terms of romantic love. But, if you consider it, the concept of romantic love barely features among the 66 books of the Bible. The two greatest “love” stories in the Bible are not of husband and wife, nor even of man and woman, but of man and man, and woman and woman: David and Jonathan, and Ruth and Naomi.

When Love Belonged to God

Instead, all love in the Bible is directed at God, and the love for the spouse, and more generally for the other, is subsumed under the love of God, of which it is an expression. Thus, in the Sacrifice of Isaac, Abraham’s love for God trumps his love for his own longed-for son Isaac, whom he is willing to sacrifice for no other reason than that God commanded it.

In ancient times, people did sometimes fall in love, but they did not believe that their love might in some sense save them, as we tend to today.

When, in the Iliad, Helen eloped with Paris, sparking the Trojan War, neither she nor he (nor anyone else) conceived of their attraction as pure or ennobling or exalting. When, in the Aeneid, Dido fell in love with Aeneas, Virgil portrays her love as a kind of divine affliction that distracts both lovers from their duties and ends in ruin and death. One might also think of Phaedra and Hippolytus, Medea and Jason, and Antony and Cleopatra.

The Rise of Romantic Love

But over the centuries, the sacred seeped out of God and into romantic love, which came to take the place of the retreating religion in lending purpose, weight, and meaning to our lives. People had once loved God, but now they loved love: more than with their beloved, they fell in love with love itself.

Abraham had surrendered himself and Isaac out of love for God. But in the Romantic era, around the time of the French Revolution, love grew into quite the opposite: a means of finding and validating oneself, of lending texture, substance, and solidity to one’s life—as encapsulated by Sylvester’s 1978 hit, You Make Me Feel (Mighty Real), the final kissing scene in Cinema Paradiso, the “You complete me” scene in Jerry Maguire, and countless other popular songs and films.

In the time of God, “finding oneself”—or, more accurately, losing oneself in God—had demanded years of patient spiritual practice. But after the French Revolution, romantic love could come to the rescue of anyone, with very little effort or sacrifice on their part. Being saved became a simple matter of luck.

If love is a word with a meaning that has changed over time, it is also a word with multiple meanings, one that points at a diversity of distinct concepts with only a family resemblance between them.

What All Love Has in Common

Unlike us, the Greeks had several words for love, enabling them to distinguish more clearly between the different types. For example, eros referred to sexual or passionate love; philia to friendship; storge to familial love; and agape to universal love, such as the love for strangers, nature, or God.

Having many more words for “love” enables us to think and talk about love in new and different ways. For example, we might say that people in the early stages of a romantic relationship often expect unconditional storge, but find only the hunger and dependency of eros, and, if they are lucky, the maturity and fertility of philia. Or, like Plato, we might say that the best kind of philia is one that is born of eros, and that in turn feeds back into eros to strengthen and develop it, transforming it from a lust for possession into an impulse for philosophy.

But if we are to understand the deep meaning of the word “love,” then we need to uncover what all these different types of love have in common. In other words, what is it that unites eros, philia, storge, and agape? What is the common element that makes them all types of love?

What all these instances of love have in common, I think, is a reaching out beyond our own being to things that are able to lend purpose, weight, and meaning to our lives, even to the point of ingesting or incorporating those things into our inner being—whence the hug, the love bite, and the sacramental bread and wine of the Eucharist.

Love is the force of nature that enables us to cross the boundary between ourselves and the world, like the lobster, to shed our shell and grow beyond it—which is why people of little love are so small.

Neel Burton is author of Heaven and Hell: The Psychology of the Emotions.

item.title: How American English Has Changed Since 1776
item.description:
Social Life

How American English Has Changed Since 1776

The sound of early America has shifted after centuries of evolution.

Posted June 28, 2026

Key points
  • Early American documents reveal clues about Colonial and Revolutionary era English pronunciation.
  • Revolutionary-era Americans had vowel and consonant distinctions that Americans have since lost.
  • American English became more diverse over time while still helping to shape a shared national identity.

Over the past 250 years, since adopting the Declaration of Independence, American life has changed in many ways the founding fathers could not have foreseen, from massive medical and technical advances to major social changes.

But what about the way Americans talk? How has our language changed since the Colonial period? What did we sound like in the days of yore?

The early American tongue

While the lack of audio recordings during this early history certainly makes listening in on America’s ancestors tricky, numerous letters, diaries, journals, and even transcripts from early legal trials can help us “listen in” on speech from earlier eras.

Spelling norms were more fluid during colonial and revolutionary times, and there are often clues to pronunciation in earlier writings, especially informal ones. For example, spellings like “dafter” for “daughter,” “Sary” for “Sarah,” “git” for “get,” and “deef” for “deaf” were common in the colonial period.

The pronunciations these spellings hint at may now sound odd, but would not have been heard the same way then. In fact, several pronunciations that today might be heard as more rustic are relics of once commonly accepted forms that are no longer in widespread use, which is why we notice them.

The coming of a revolution

Benjamin Franklin invented a phonetic alphabet.
Source: WikiImages/Pixabay

We also have a few clues to pronunciation from writings left behind by people like Noah Webster, who compiled the first truly American dictionary, and Benjamin Franklin, one of the founding fathers. Franklin even devised and used a phonetic alphabet, which helps us understand how he and other people of the revolutionary era spoke.

From such sources, we can glean that the “h” sound originally heard at the beginning of words like “which,” “when,” and “whale” was still pronounced during that time, as in “huh-wich” or “huh-wen.” Some Americans, for example, in the U.S. South, still use these pronunciations.

Likewise, the "t" sound that comes out more like “d” in American English in words like “water,” “later,” “patty,” or “atom” were not yet regularly “flapped,” as linguists call it, meaning it would have been said like a “t,” as in “a-tom” rather than “a-dom.”

Tomay-to or tomah-to?

These consonant differences are fascinating, but most likely, a time traveler going back to 1776 would probably notice vowel differences the most.

In Colonial times, American vowels may have sounded more like what we hear in some of today’s dialects from the British Isles, such as Irish English. For example, the “ey” vowel (as in “day”) and the “oh” vowel (as in “no”) were both shorter, simpler vowels at the time, sounding a bit more like “deh” and “gnaw.”

There were also a number of vowel distinctions that most Americans no longer make today.

“Horse” and “hoarse” were pronounced differently then (hence, the different spellings), with “hoarse” sounding a bit more like “hoe-erse.” Similarly, the vowels in “fir” and “fur” were said as separate vowels by pretty much all speakers in that era.

And then there’s “merry” and “marry.” Back then, most people in America would have said those words differently. Nowadays, the vowels in these words are merged together for many Americans, while some others keep them separate, for example, people in our nation’s first capital, Philadelphia, as well as in New York.

Another notable difference is that the vowel in words like “right” or “life” would have sounded more like “oy,” as in “roy-t” or “loy-f” in that time. This pronunciation still lingers in some eastern coastal areas like Martha’s Vineyard, Massachusetts, or Tangier Island, Virginia.

Finally, Americans would not have pronounced words like “aunt” or “rather” with an “ah” at that time, but neither would many British speakers. The “ah” we hear in Southern British “ahnt” and “rah-ther” didn’t become popular in England until the late 18th or early 19th century, and so would not have been picked up in any American varieties quite yet.

A nation first united, then divided

In early colonial era writings, many observers noted that speech across the colonies was surprisingly uniform compared to the vast diversity of dialects heard back home in Britain.

But by the time of the Revolution, regional differences appeared to be growing. Noah Webster remarked that there was a bit of a nasal whine heard among New Englanders and also commented on the regional pronunciation of “serve” as “sarve.”

Webster also noted a mid-Atlantic tendency to pronounce words like “off” and “drop” more like “aff” and “drap” and notes that some rural Easterners say words with the “aw” vowel (like “power” or “out”) with an “ih” sound first: “pi-ower.”

As for Southern states, Webster mentions that Virginians sometimes didn’t pronounce all their “r” sounds (in words like “cart”), likely following the fledgling new fashion of dropping "r" sounds in London speech.

A nation united

Regional distinctions like this were viewed with concern by Noah Webster and the founding fathers, who felt a single American “language” would help mark independence from Britain and keep the states unified.

There was also great concern expressed in the post-Revolutionary era about the large number of non-English-speaking people in the U.S. Ben Franklin, for one, openly fretted about the negative influence languages like French and German, which were quite prevalent in the Colonial U.S., would have on American English.

What the American English of today attests, though, is that instead of decay or destruction from the passing of time and contact with other languages, American English has grown and thrived. Early American English arose as a blend of earlier British dialects and the languages of Continental Europeans, Native Americans, and Africans, and it has since evolved to embrace linguistic influences from across the globe.

And nowadays, our rich array of American dialects, including both native and non-native varieties, is a reflection of the diversity out of which the strong fabric of our united nation is woven. “Out of many, one” is a perfect motto for our country’s languages and dialects, just as it is for our people.

item.title: The Importance of Empathy in Treating Seniors for Depression
item.description:
Depression

The Importance of Empathy in Treating Seniors for Depression

Depression is too often ignored in older adults and the results can be tragic.

Posted June 28, 2026

Key points
  • The empathic connection when treating older people cannot be overstated.
  • Teasing apart symptoms to determine if they're signs of depression or dementia requires a full consultation.
  • The result of not detecting or treating depression can be devastating.
Source: Tima Miroshnichenko/Pexels

The relational aspect of working with older patients cannot, in my experience, be overstated. When seniors start psychotherapy, they are almost always eager to use their time productively and, have a lot to say. They have lived through painful emotional experiences, illness, family and financial difficulties, and loss. Many have never set aside time to share and explore their feelings and memories. Frequently, they live alone, feel isolated, and are especially appreciative of the psychotherapeutic opportunity.

It's hardly a surprise that a good doctor-patient relationship is key to successful treatment. But with the emphasis today, in the increasingly corporatized medical industry, on increasing the volume of patients one sees, medical appointments are often brief and businesslike. And while the signs and symptoms of depression can be very clear in a younger person, with someone who is elderly, teasing apart what is causing their problems requires a bit of detective work.

Before bringing in her mother to see me, Nancy, her adult daughter, told me, "I don't know what's going on with my mom. Until a few years ago, she was calm, organized, and thoughtful. Now she's an anxious, irritable, indecisive old lady," Nancy said. "Sometimes I think she's losing it. At other times, I'm convinced she is just plain nasty and hateful and deliberately wants to torture us with her mean comments and impatience."

Nancy's description of her 84-year-old mother is similar to many complaints I hear from adult children who are concerned and, often, fed up with their elderly parents. When seniors, like Nancy's mom, show signs of cognitive decline (difficulty staying focused, planning, making decisions or problem solving, for instance), moodiness (irritability or apathy, for example), or somatic problems (not sleeping or eating well), there is always a question as to whether these are part of the typical symptom package of depression, independent of it, or overlap with it. Since memory loss, apathy, and cognitive problems can be signs of depression as well as dementia, it is only with a comprehensive consultation that a health practitioner can determine what is causing these symptoms.

The Danger of Undiagnosed or Misdiagnosed Depression

The results of not detecting and not treating depression can be tragic. "Suicide is one of the leading causes of death in the U.S., and rates are on the rise—especially among people age 65 and over," according to the National Council on Aging. While older adults comprise just 16.8% of the population, they made up approximately 22% of suicides in 2022.

Depression is too often ignored in older adults. There are many situational factors that affect seniors--chronic medical conditions, mobility problems, living alone and suffering from isolation—which can be pointed to as causing shifts in mood and personality. Many people prefer to rationalize their reactions to these real-life challenges and avoid the stigma of being identified with a psychiatric diagnosis. But signs of depression should never be neglected. Depression may be the most likely cause of cognitive decline as we get older. The same chemicals that mediate mood also mediate memory. It's not uncommon for cognitive function to improve significantly once treated for depression. In fact, even if someone is diagnosed with Alzheimer’s or a related dementia, it’s important to rule out depression, as depression can accompany (and also be an early sign of) dementia.

The Importance of Seniors Feeling Seen

Those who are elderly often feel invisible. They don't feel seen, heard, or cared about in our society. When a diagnosis is made of depression, the cognitive, emotional, and physical symptoms will usually respond to antidepressive treatment, even if it takes some trial and error to determine the right combination and dosage of drugs. But, whether because of the stigma associated with psychiatry or just general defiance, many seniors don't want to take antidepressants that are prescribed to them.

That's another reason why the bond with the patient is so important. Taking the time to develop trust with a patient leads to less or even no resistance to following a treatment plan. It's not just what psychiatric drug is prescribed but how it is prescribed and how a patient feels about their practitioner who prescribes it that makes the difference as to whether they will have a successful outcome of treatment.

Once there is trust between patient and doctor a treatment plan can be created that the patient will believe in. Just as an older person who suffers from diabetes or high cholesterol needs to take their medication so, too, should they take the appropriate psychotropic medication so they can live as optimally as possible. Helping family members understand the nature of the patient's condition and how best to approach them is also critical.

Communicating with Family Members

Just as establishing an empathic connection with patients is key, so, too, is (with the patient's permission) developing a supportive relationship with family members who are often angry at their loved one for constantly repeating themselves, needing things to be repeated, or just plain forgetting things that were said or happened.

It's important for loved ones to understand when depression is contributing to or causing cognitive decline. And, if there is still cognitive slippage after treating depression, families must be helped to understand that dementia may be a contributing factor, that cognitive decline is a slow progression, and that the patient must be assisted—not blamed—in handling their condition. Modeling empathy to patient and family sets a foundation for an optimal response to diagnosis and treatment as well as the ability of relatives to empathically connect with their loved one as they navigate this challenging time in their lives.

item.title: How Unnamed Needs Can Keep Us Stuck in a Drinking Loop
item.description:
Alcoholism

How Unnamed Needs Can Keep Us Stuck in a Drinking Loop

Looking beyond problem drinking: Alcohol as an attempt to meet unnamed needs.

Posted June 28, 2026

Key points
  • Alcohol use often fills unnamed needs, not just causes problems, which can keep us stuck in a loop.
  • Attempts to quit often fail when we ignore the roles alcohol plays, not just its negative effects.
  • Reframing drinking as a failed solution, not a flaw, can enable deeper self-compassion and insight.

“Why is it so hard to quit drinking?” I used to ask.

I had a full list of good reasons why I should quit:

  • The blackout and hangover.
  • The missed work and the promises I failed to keep.
  • The hurtful words I’d spill and the embarrassing actions I’d commit after the second bottle of wine.

The list goes on, and yet somehow, I kept finding myself having another drink.

I thought I must be broken; how else could I explain repeatedly doing something I knew was hurting me?

It took me years to realize that it wasn't the drink itself that I kept reaching for; it was what the drink did for me that kept pulling me back.

The mistake: My drinking is nothing but a problem to be solved

Today, as I guide others to outgrow their old drinking patterns, I have come to see that one of the most common mistakes that holds many people back when they try to change their relationship with alcohol is the same one that once kept me stuck: seeing our drinking as nothing but a problem to be solved.

It makes sense. By the time alcohol starts to draw attention in our lives, it’s often because of the issues it has caused: blackouts, hangovers, and health concerns. It’s natural for us to conclude that drinking does nothing good for us, and we need to stop it.

However, when we try to quit or cut down, many of us find that breaking old drinking patterns is not as simple as we hoped it would be. So we feel confused, frustrated, and even ashamed—if we already know a behavior is hurting us, why can’t we stop doing it? It’s easy to feel that something must be wrong with us.

But here is something that most of us miss: Long before drinking became a problem, it may have first been a solution.

The reframe: Before it became a problem, it was first a solution

The truth is: what we are struggling to let go of is not alcohol itself, but what alcohol has been doing for us.

  • We don't drink at a friend's birthday party hoping to wake up with only fragments of the night; we drink to feel more social, connected, or less anxious.
  • We don't pour ourselves a drink after work hoping to say something we'd regret; we drink to switch off our working brain and finally relax.
  • We don't reach for wine on a Sunday afternoon hoping to damage our liver years from now; we drink to escape stress, boredom, or emptiness for a little while.

In other words, what we are reaching back for is often not the drink itself, but the role the drink has come to play in our lives.

It’s not the “problem” that keeps pulling us back; it’s the “solutions.”

The mainstream narrative: The unintentional false dichotomies

This realization fundamentally changed the way I understand our struggle with alcohol. Instead of asking, "What's wrong with me?" I started asking, "What is alcohol doing for me?"

When it comes to alcohol, throughout history, we have been told many stories about why a person would struggle to let it go. Once upon a time, we believed it was due to moral failure and weak character. Over time, we began to see it as a disease or a malfunctioning brain.

However, each explanation often unintentionally fosters the false dichotomies of “normal” vs. “problematic” and “well” vs. sick. And both have overlooked one simple explanation: because alcohol is doing something for the person.

Once you learn how to look beyond the surface and see beneath the behavior, you will see that there is almost never a person who drinks out of a pure desire to ruin their life. Drinking, in its own way, however counterproductive it might have become, was initially an attempt to address another unnamed and unmet need.

  • When you look beyond the party beer bong, you may find a shy college student who learned to use alcohol to get out of their shell and socialize.
  • When you see beyond the nightly wine, you may find an exhausted woman who learned to use alcohol as a way to finally slow down and rest.
  • When you look beyond the Sunday afternoon scotch, you may find a retired man who learned to use alcohol to fill up the empty hours.

Beneath the apparent “drinking problem,” there is a need to fit in and connect, to slow down and rest, or to be stimulated and feel alive.

The invisible force that fuels the drinking loop: Unnamed needs

The Invisible Drinking Loop
Source: Jeanette Hu

Today, I call these invisible needs that fuel our drinking patterns unnamed needs. They are the first force in what I call the Invisible Drinking Loop.

As long as these needs remain unnamed and unaddressed, the pull toward old drinking patterns will often remain.

So the next time you find yourself wanting a drink despite knowing that alcohol is causing problems in your life, instead of beating yourself up or asking, "What's wrong with me?", I invite you to turn toward yourself with compassionate curiosity and ask:

What does alcohol do for me?

Because what often leads to lasting change is not shame and blame, but compassion and understanding.

If you would like to understand your relationship with alcohol through a more compassionate lens, you can find more reading like this at the Beyond Alcohol Project.

item.title: 'Hustle Culture' Is Leading Us to Burnout
item.description:
Burnout

'Hustle Culture' Is Leading Us to Burnout

Current messaging about productivity is worsening burnout for many people.

Posted June 28, 2026

Key points
  • "Hustle culture" makes an already-complicated daily existence busier and less open to mindfulness.
  • Current social media trends promote an unhealthy attachment to productivity.
  • Longstanding norms of hyper-productivity are leading to increased rates of burnout.

The irony should not be lost on us: optimizing and maximizing, two words we are hearing more and more in the current life-advice social media zeitgeist, are actually resulting in exhaustion and burnout, virtually defeating their intended purpose of increasing productivity and reaching a state of ultimate effectiveness.

From “wellnessmaxxing,” the idea of optimizing self-care, to “biohacking,” the idea of intervening in natural bodily functions (such as sleep) to “hack” or maximize physical functioning, to “habit stacking,” the idea of adding a new habit to an already established one, there are a multitude of buzzy, trendy ways to reach optimal daily functioning. And these trends are to say nothing about longer-standing problematic optimization standards like blurry work boundaries and constant digital connectivity.

How 'Hustle Culture' Adds Stress Instead of Relief

While we may, in fact, be living in a time of unprecedented daily optimization, the downside of this “hustle culture” is that it can make an already complicated, overwhelming, and stressful daily existence even busier, more outcome-oriented, and less open to mindfulness and presence.

American workforce burnout reached an all-time high with nearly 72 percent of U.S. workers reporting moderate to severe levels of workplace burnout in 2025 (Mohr et al., 2025). Three out of every four Americans are feeling tired, overburdened, stretched thin, and burnt out.

Our relationships with our jobs are part of the problem, but we might argue that another part is the overarching messaging of “hustle,” “optimize,” “be productive,” and “maximize” that we hear daily, both directly and indirectly. Repeated often enough, a message can be accepted and go unchallenged. But, for the sake of our collective mental health, the message of hyper-productivity that has long been perpetuated by American culture must be challenged and changed.

Historical Roots

In psychological circles, we might trace some of this messaging back to the early self-improvement literature, which offered titles such as The Laws of Success, How to Win Friends and Influence People, Think and Grow Rich, and The Master Key System. These titles were early precursors to the current culture of optimization—here is how to win, get rich, and be successful. The content of these books was rarely based on psychological theory, and often provided dubious, albeit bestselling blueprints for quick maximization.

Social Media and the Unending Push for Life Hacks

Many of the most popular optimization-based TikTok reels sound eerily similar to these old book titles: “How to Stop Procrastinating in Two Minutes,” “How to Reset Your Brain,” “How to Win Every Day,” “Leverage Your Mind.” The overarching message is the same: You can hack life by learning how to optimize your existence. This, however, comes with an unspoken caveat: We must be constantly training our brains, learning new hacks, and unlocking new shortcuts—rather than simply living our lives, we are forever striving to make them better, easier, more comfortable, and more monetarily sustainable.

Healthy Self-Improvement From Craving-Based Striving

Let me make an important distinction: Aiming to improve our lives is, of course, not an inherently bad thing and is, indeed, much of what is focused on in the therapy room. There are healthy, adaptive, and psychologically based ways to do this. The problem is that our culture of optimization presents the goal of improvement as a constant striving. Buddhist tenets present an important differentiation between striving that is based on craving and striving that is based on “right effort.” Craving-based striving might be doing something in order to achieve more status, whereas “right effort” striving might be doing something for our long-term betterment or health (Bodhi, 1994).

Unfortunately, many of the optimization and maximization reels that are popular on social media platforms are undeniably craving-based, to wit: “How to Win Every Day.” The Buddhists would argue that craving leads to suffering, and one of the types of suffering we face in our modern world comes in the form of burnout.

The Need for Mindfulness Amidst Hustle Culture

In my clinical practice, I find myself talking more and more about mindfulness and slowing down. So many clients I see report feeling overwhelmed, burned out, and exhausted by the constant hustle and striving that has become the norm in our society. External messages have a lot of power to influence how we conduct our lives and what habits we adopt. It is important to be willing to challenge some of these messages, particularly those that lead us to negative states like burnout.

It is human nature to desire improvement and to want to better our circumstances, but the way we go about trying to achieve this dictates whether it helps or hurts us. Our current culture of optimization is accomplishing the opposite of its intended purpose: Rather than making our lives easier, it is adding more to our plates, which statistics show are already overfilled.

item.title: Heat Can Make Driving Deadly
item.description:
Cognition

Heat Can Make Driving Deadly

High temperatures can impair driver performance and increase fatal accident rates.

Posted June 28, 2026

Key points
  • Traffic fatality rates are around 9% higher on hot days compared to mild-temperature days.
  • Heat can impair driver judgment, slow reaction times, and increase speeding and aggressive driving.
  • Risk extends to pedestrians and cyclists, who are also affected by heat and less protected.

Over 1 million people die in traffic accidents every year. According to the WHO Global Status Report on Road Safety 2023, the figure was 1.19 million in 2021 alone. The numbers have been declining in recent years, reflecting improvements in road and vehicle safety. But the human toll remains unacceptably high. As of 2019, road traffic crashes were still the leading cause of death among children and young people between 5 and 29 years of age, and the 12th leading cause of death overall.

No matter how much road and vehicle safety improve, the human factor will always be harder to control. And there are reasons to think that this particular dimension may be getting worse.

The reason is the increase in extreme heat events around the world.

In recent posts, we discussed how heat clouds people's thinking, resulting in poor decisions, and lowers impulse control, resulting in more violent crime. Put those two facts together, and the implications for driving become clear. When judgment is impaired and impulses take over, the consequences behind the wheel can be severe.

Sometimes, phrases like "impaired judgment" or "impulsive decision-making" sound too abstract. Consider what they look like in traffic: speeding; turning without signaling; impatient overtaking; ignoring blind spots; road rage; reversing without checking; tailgating; jaywalking. Less abstract now?

Driving Under the Influence of Heat

The effects of extreme heat on driving have been known for decades. Research from the 1970s and 1980s already showed that high temperatures reduce attention span and increase driver fatigue, sometimes leading to drowsiness. Extreme heat impairs cognitive functions and increases risky behaviours such as speeding and aggressive driving. It also decreases reaction times and makes drivers more prone to distraction. Further, sun glare can reduce visibility.

All these factors add up and increase the risk of accidents. What has changed in recent years is not the relationship between extreme heat and traffic accidents. It is simply that extreme heat days are becoming more frequent, making the problem more severe. Ongoing improvements in vehicle and road safety may be masking this trend.

More Traffic Fatalities on Hot Days

Research studies looking at traffic accidents under different weather conditions can tell us whether high temperatures have a relevant effect on traffic accidents and fatalities. And those studies speak a clear language. For example, research reported by Resources for the Future, a nonpartisan think tank focused on environmental and resource economics, sheds light on the scale of the effect. Leard and Roth (2017) studied weather and traffic accidents using records from over 46 million police-reported accidents, including over a quarter million fatalities, in the United States. They found that on days with temperatures above 80°F (27°C), traffic fatality rates were 8.6% higher compared to days in the 50–60°F range (10–16°C).

Not all of this is due to drivers becoming more reckless, though. A large part of the effect in the data of Leard and Roth could be attributed to greater exposure: on hot days, more pedestrians, cyclists, and bikers are out, and they are less protected. The rest of the effect, however, is likely due to increased driver recklessness. Both factors are also likely to compound, as greater exposure means that the consequences of every additional accident due to driver error are likely to be more severe.

A study of over 100,000 motor vehicle crashes in Spain, by Basagaña and coauthors (2015), found that crash risk increased by 2.9% during heat wave days overall. But when looking only at crashes caused by driver errors, the increase was 7.7%, confirming that reduced driver performance is a major driver behind the problem.

In the same study, the risk of a crash due to driver error increased by 1.1% for each 1°C rise in maximum temperature. Similar results have been found worldwide. Park and coauthors (2021), using data from South Korea between 2012 and 2017, found that traffic accidents increased by approximately 0.6% per 1°C rise in daily maximum temperature. Gariazzo and coauthors (2021) used high-resolution road crash and temperature data from Italy between 2013 and 2015 and found that crash risk escalated markedly on extreme hot days, defined roughly as the hottest 25% of days. Those “extreme” days of the 2010s, however, may soon become the new normal.

What Can You Do?

Once it is clear that heat clouds judgment and increases impulsivity, it follows that driving on extreme-heat days or during heat waves is riskier than usual. Even if you stay cool, hydrated, and use air conditioning sensibly, other drivers, pedestrians, and cyclists around you may not. Their impairment raises your risk too.

Awareness is the first step toward safety. Whether you drive, ride, or walk, on hot days, assume that everyone around you has a shorter attention span and slower reactions. Give people more space. Do not assume they have seen you, or that they will brake in time.

Exposure compounds the problem. If you ride a motorbike, bicycle, or electric scooter, wear a helmet. Regardless of what the law requires, choosing not to wear a helmet when you are that exposed in traffic is not a lifestyle preference: it is a risk you should not take. The temptation to skip it is strongest when it is hot, but that is also when the danger may be highest.

Finally, assume that you, too, are operating with a reduced attention span and slower reactions. Increase the distance to the car in front of you, in case you need to brake. Reduce your usual speed by around 20%. If the heat is severe and you commute by car, speak to your employer about working from home or shifting your hours to avoid peak traffic.

Most drivers believe they are better than most other drivers (which is a statistical impossibility, but never mind that). Even if it were true, heat does not discriminate: you are a worse driver when it’s hot.

Safe driving, everyone.
